report:
**Conclusion:** 
Your assessment is correct: the claim that increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes an increase in autism is false and unsupported by scientific evidence.

**Evidence:**
1. **No Link to Antigen Exposure:** Rigorous medical studies have evaluated whether receiving multiple vaccines—and thus higher cumulative exposure to antibody-stimulating proteins and polysaccharides—increases the risk of autism. Findings show that total antigen exposure from childhood vaccines given from birth to age two is not associated with an increased risk of developing autism spectrum disorder (https://www.cdc.gov/vaccine-safety/about/autism.html?CDC_AAref_Val=https://www.cdc.gov/vaccinesafety/concerns/autism.html, https://www.jpeds.com/article/S0022-3476(13)00144-3/abstract?ext=.pdf)).
2. **Fraudulent Origin of the Claim:** The popular myth linking childhood vaccination to autism stems from a small 1998 paper by Andrew Wakefield and colleagues. The study was subsequently shown to be fraudulent, thoroughly refuted by numerous large-scale global studies, and fully retracted by *The Lancet* (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3136032/).
3. **Broad Scientific Consensus:** Extensive research over more than two decades by leading public health and scientific organizations confirms that vaccines and vaccine schedules do not cause autism (https://www.autismspeaks.org/do-vaccines-cause-autism).

**Sources:**
- CDC Vaccine Safety: https://www.cdc.gov/vaccine-safety/about/autism.html?CDC_AAref_Val=https://www.cdc.gov/vaccinesafety/concerns/autism.html
- The Journal of Pediatrics: https://www.jpeds.com/article/S0022-3476(13)00144-3/abstract?ext=.pdf)
- PMC Overview on MMR Vaccine & Autism: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3136032/
- Autism Speaks: https://www.autismspeaks.org/do-vaccines-cause-autism
